title: Music Theory: Intervals, Scales, Chords, Terms

sources.name: Open Music Theory, open educational reference

description: For beginners studying Western music notation and tonal theory: intervals, scales, chords, meter, rhythm, dynamics, texture, and form. Examples use letter names and standard twelve-tone equal-tempered semitone counts.

cards.back: The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, closely related to its frequency.
cards.example: A faster-vibrating tone is generally heard as a higher pitch.

cards.back: A grouping of pitches related by octaves, such as all C notes.
cards.example: C3 and C5 share the pitch class C.

cards.back: An interval spanning eight diatonic letter names; in standard tuning, the higher frequency is twice the lower.
cards.example: A4 at 440 Hz and A5 at 880 Hz are an octave apart.

cards.back: A set of five horizontal lines and four spaces used to indicate pitches in standard notation.
cards.example: Notes on different lines and spaces represent different pitches.

cards.back: A short additional staff line used for notes above or below the main staff.
cards.example: Middle C uses a ledger line below the treble staff.

cards.back: The G clef normally placing G4 on the second staff line from the bottom.
cards.example: The treble-clef lines from bottom to top are E4, G4, B4, D5, F5.

cards.back: The F clef normally placing F3 on the fourth staff line from the bottom.
cards.example: The bass-clef lines from bottom to top are G2, B2, D3, F3, A3.

cards.back: A C clef placing middle C on the middle staff line.
cards.example: Viola parts commonly use alto clef.

cards.back: A C clef placing middle C on the fourth staff line from the bottom.
cards.example: Cello parts may use tenor clef in a higher register.

cards.back: Treble and bass staves joined for one instrumental part, commonly piano.
cards.example: A pianist often reads right-hand notes above left-hand notes on a grand staff.

cards.front: What is Middle C in scientific pitch notation?
cards.back: C4, with octave numbers changing at C in scientific pitch notation.
cards.example: The C just below D4 is C4.

cards.back: A sign that alters a note from the pitch otherwise indicated by the staff and key signature.
cards.example: A sharp before F raises it to F-sharp.

cards.back: An accidental that raises a note by one semitone.
cards.example: F-sharp is one semitone above F-natural.

cards.back: An accidental that lowers a note by one semitone.
cards.example: B-flat is one semitone below B-natural.

cards.back: An accidental indicating the unsharpened and unflattened form of a letter-named note.
cards.example: A natural before B cancels B-flat for that note under ordinary notation rules.

cards.back: An accidental raising a letter-named note by two semitones.
cards.example: F-double-sharp sounds like G-natural in twelve-tone equal temperament.

cards.back: An accidental lowering a letter-named note by two semitones.
cards.example: B-double-flat sounds like A-natural in twelve-tone equal temperament.

cards.back: Differently spelled notes that sound alike in twelve-tone equal temperament but may serve different musical functions.
cards.example: C-sharp and D-flat are enharmonic equivalents.

cards.back: The smallest step in the standard twelve-tone equal-tempered chromatic scale; also called a half step.
cards.example: E to F is a semitone.

cards.back: An interval of two semitones; also called a whole step.
cards.example: C to D is a whole tone.

cards.back: The seven repeating note letters A, B, C, D, E, F, and G.
cards.example: After G, the letter sequence returns to A.

cards.back: Sharps or flats written at the beginning of a staff to establish default alterations for note letters.
cards.example: One sharp in a standard key signature alters F throughout the staff.

cards.front: What is Order of sharps in standard key signatures?
cards.back: F, C, G, D, A, E, B.
cards.example: A three-sharp signature contains F-sharp, C-sharp, and G-sharp.

cards.front: What is Order of flats in standard key signatures?
cards.back: B, E, A, D, G, C, F.
cards.example: A three-flat signature contains B-flat, E-flat, and A-flat.

cards.back: A line dividing music into measures.
cards.example: In 4/4, a full ordinary measure contains four quarter-note beats.

cards.back: A segment of notated music between bar lines; also called a bar.
cards.example: Four quarter notes fill a normal 4/4 measure.

cards.back: A curved line joining notes of the same pitch so their durations combine into one sustained sound.
cards.example: Two tied quarter notes last as long as a half note.

cards.back: A curved line grouping notes for smooth or connected performance; instrument-specific technique may vary.
cards.example: A phrase under a slur is played legato.

cards.back: A symbol indicating a measured duration of silence.
cards.example: A quarter rest occupies the same duration as a quarter note.

cards.back: A sign asking the performer to hold a note or rest longer than its written duration, as context directs.
cards.example: A final chord with a fermata may be sustained before release.

cards.back: The distance between two pitches sounded in succession.
cards.example: C followed by E forms a melodic third.

cards.back: The distance between two pitches sounded simultaneously.
cards.example: C and E played together form a harmonic third.

cards.back: The number of letter-name positions spanned, counting both endpoints.
cards.example: C to F spans C, D, E, F and is a fourth.

cards.back: A label such as perfect, major, minor, augmented, or diminished that specifies an interval's size beyond its number.
cards.example: C to E is a major third; C to E-flat is a minor third.

cards.back: Two notes with the same letter name and pitch, separated by zero semitones.
cards.example: C4 to C4 is a perfect unison.

cards.back: An interval of one semitone with adjacent letter names.
cards.example: E to F is a minor second.

cards.back: An interval of two semitones with adjacent letter names.
cards.example: C to D is a major second.

cards.back: An interval of three semitones spanning three letter names.
cards.example: C to E-flat is a minor third.

cards.back: An interval of four semitones spanning three letter names.
cards.example: C to E is a major third.

cards.back: An interval of five semitones spanning four letter names.
cards.example: C to F is a perfect fourth.

cards.back: A fourth widened to six semitones.
cards.example: C to F-sharp is an augmented fourth.

cards.back: A fifth narrowed to six semitones.
cards.example: C to G-flat is a diminished fifth.

cards.back: An interval of seven semitones spanning five letter names.
cards.example: C to G is a perfect fifth.

cards.back: An interval of eight semitones spanning six letter names.
cards.example: C to A-flat is a minor sixth.

cards.back: An interval of nine semitones spanning six letter names.
cards.example: C to A is a major sixth.

cards.back: An interval of ten semitones spanning seven letter names.
cards.example: C to B-flat is a minor seventh.

cards.back: An interval of eleven semitones spanning seven letter names.
cards.example: C to B is a major seventh.

cards.back: An interval of twelve semitones spanning eight letter positions.
cards.example: C4 to C5 is a perfect octave.

cards.back: An interval of six semitones, commonly spelled as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth.
cards.example: F to B is an augmented fourth and a tritone.

cards.back: An interval larger than an octave.
cards.example: C4 to D5 is a major ninth.

cards.back: Moving an interval's lower note up an octave or upper note down an octave, reversing their order.
cards.example: C below E becomes E below C, changing a major third to a minor sixth.

cards.front: What is Number rule for simple interval inversions?
cards.back: The interval numbers add to nine under the usual inversion convention.
cards.example: A third inverts to a sixth.

cards.front: What is Quality rule for interval inversions?
cards.back: Major becomes minor, minor becomes major, perfect stays perfect, and augmented and diminished exchange.
cards.example: A perfect fourth inverts to a perfect fifth.

cards.back: A context-dependent sense of relative stability or repose between pitches.
cards.example: A major triad often functions as a stable harmony in tonal music.

cards.back: A context-dependent sense of tension or instability between pitches.
cards.example: A seventh above a chord's bass often seeks resolution in common-practice harmony.

cards.back: An ordered collection of pitches, usually described within an octave.
cards.example: C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C forms C major.

cards.front: What is Major scale step pattern?
cards.back: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
cards.example: C major has half steps from E to F and B to C.

cards.front: What is Natural minor scale step pattern?
cards.back: Whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole.
cards.example: A natural minor is A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A.

cards.back: A natural minor scale with its seventh degree raised by one semitone.
cards.example: A harmonic minor uses G-sharp instead of G.

cards.front: What is Classical melodic minor scale?
cards.back: Conventionally, natural minor with raised sixth and seventh degrees ascending, and natural minor descending.
cards.example: A melodic minor ascends with F-sharp and G-sharp and descends with G and F.

cards.front: What is Jazz melodic minor scale?
cards.back: A minor scale with raised sixth and seventh degrees, commonly used in the same form ascending and descending.
cards.example: A jazz melodic minor uses A, B, C, D, E, F-sharp, G-sharp.

cards.back: A five-note scale corresponding to degrees 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 of a major scale.
cards.example: C major pentatonic is C, D, E, G, A.

cards.back: A five-note scale commonly described as 1, flat 3, 4, 5, flat 7 relative to major.
cards.example: A minor pentatonic is A, C, D, E, G.

cards.front: What is Six-note minor blues scale?
cards.back: A minor pentatonic scale with an added flat fifth.
cards.example: A blues is A, C, D, E-flat, E, G.

cards.back: A scale containing all twelve pitch classes, moving by semitones.
cards.example: A chromatic ascent from C includes C-sharp, D, and D-sharp.

cards.back: A six-note scale made entirely of whole steps.
cards.example: C, D, E, F-sharp, G-sharp, A-sharp forms a whole-tone collection.

cards.back: The first scale degree and tonal center of a key.
cards.example: C is the tonic of C major.

cards.back: The second scale degree.
cards.example: D is the supertonic of C major.

cards.back: The third scale degree.
cards.example: E is the mediant of C major.

cards.back: The fourth scale degree.
cards.example: F is the subdominant of C major.

cards.back: The fifth scale degree.
cards.example: G is the dominant of C major.

cards.back: The sixth scale degree.
cards.example: A is the submediant of C major.

cards.back: The seventh scale degree when it lies a semitone below the tonic.
cards.example: B is the leading tone in C major.

cards.back: The seventh scale degree when it lies a whole tone below the tonic.
cards.example: G is the subtonic in A natural minor.

cards.front: What is Relative major and minor keys?
cards.back: A major and minor key that share a key signature; the minor tonic is the major scale's sixth degree.
cards.example: C major and A minor are relative keys.

cards.front: What is Parallel major and minor keys?
cards.back: Major and minor keys sharing the same tonic.
cards.example: C major and C minor are parallel keys.

cards.back: An arrangement of keys or pitch classes by successive perfect fifths, useful for visualizing key signatures and relationships.
cards.example: C to G to D adds one sharp at each step among these major keys.

cards.back: The mode with the same interval pattern as the major scale.
cards.example: C Ionian uses the white-key notes from C to C.

cards.back: A minor-type mode with a natural sixth: 1, 2, flat 3, 4, 5, 6, flat 7 relative to major.
cards.example: D Dorian is D, E, F, G, A, B, C.

cards.back: A minor-type mode with a flat second: 1, flat 2, flat 3, 4, 5, flat 6, flat 7.
cards.example: E Phrygian is E, F, G, A, B, C, D.

cards.back: A major-type mode with a raised fourth: 1, 2, 3, sharp 4, 5, 6, 7.
cards.example: F Lydian is F, G, A, B, C, D, E.

cards.back: A major-type mode with a flat seventh: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, flat 7.
cards.example: G Mixolydian is G, A, B, C, D, E, F.

cards.back: The mode with the same pattern as the natural minor scale.
cards.example: A Aeolian uses A, B, C, D, E, F, G.

cards.back: A mode with degrees 1, flat 2, flat 3, 4, flat 5, flat 6, flat 7 relative to major.
cards.example: B Locrian is B, C, D, E, F, G, A.

cards.back: Music drawing mainly on the notes of a particular diatonic scale or key context.
cards.example: F-natural is diatonic to C major.

cards.back: Use of a pitch changed from the diatonic collection of the current key.
cards.example: F-sharp is a chromatic alteration in C major.

cards.back: A three-note chord built from a root, third, and fifth in tertian harmony.
cards.example: C, E, G form a C major triad.

cards.back: A root, major third, and perfect fifth; semitone positions 0, 4, 7 above the root.
cards.example: C, E, G form C major.

cards.back: A root, minor third, and perfect fifth; semitone positions 0, 3, 7.
cards.example: C, E-flat, G form C minor.

cards.back: A root, minor third, and diminished fifth; semitone positions 0, 3, 6.
cards.example: C, E-flat, G-flat form C diminished.

cards.back: A root, major third, and augmented fifth; semitone positions 0, 4, 8.
cards.example: C, E, G-sharp form C augmented.

cards.back: The pitch on which a chord's identity and stacked-third structure are based; it need not be the lowest sounding note.
cards.example: In E, G, C, the root of the C major chord is C.

cards.back: The lowest sounding note of a chord or texture.
cards.example: E is the bass in a C major chord voiced E, G, C.

cards.back: A triad with its root in the bass.
cards.example: C, E, G with C lowest is C major in root position.

cards.back: A triad with its third in the bass.
cards.example: E, G, C with E lowest is first-inversion C major.

cards.back: A triad with its fifth in the bass.
cards.example: G, C, E with G lowest is second-inversion C major.

cards.back: A chord containing a root, third, fifth, and seventh in tertian harmony.
cards.example: C, E, G, B form a C major seventh chord.

cards.back: A major triad plus a major seventh above the root; 0, 4, 7, 11 semitones.
cards.example: Cmaj7 contains C, E, G, B.

cards.front: What is Dominant seventh chord quality?
cards.back: A major triad plus a minor seventh; 0, 4, 7, 10 semitones, whether or not functioning as a dominant in context.
cards.example: C7 contains C, E, G, B-flat.

cards.back: A minor triad plus a minor seventh; 0, 3, 7, 10 semitones.
cards.example: Cm7 contains C, E-flat, G, B-flat.

cards.back: A diminished triad plus a minor seventh; 0, 3, 6, 10 semitones.
cards.example: Cm7 flat 5 contains C, E-flat, G-flat, B-flat.

cards.front: What is Fully diminished seventh chord?
cards.back: A diminished triad plus a diminished seventh; 0, 3, 6, 9 semitones.
cards.example: C diminished seventh contains C, E-flat, G-flat, B-double-flat.

cards.back: A chord commonly containing root, perfect fourth, and perfect fifth, with the third omitted or replaced.
cards.example: Csus4 contains C, F, G.

cards.back: A chord commonly containing root, major second, and perfect fifth, with no third.
cards.example: Csus2 contains C, D, G.

cards.back: A major or minor triad with an added sixth, commonly a major sixth above the root.
cards.example: C6 contains C, E, G, A.

cards.back: A triad with an added ninth but no implied seventh.
cards.example: Cadd9 contains C, E, G, D.

cards.back: The notes of a chord played in succession rather than all together.
cards.example: C, E, G, C played one after another outlines C major.

cards.front: What is Roman numerals in harmonic analysis?
cards.back: Symbols showing a chord's scale-degree root and usually its quality through case and added signs.
cards.example: In C major, V commonly labels a G major chord.

cards.front: What is Diatonic triad qualities in a major key?
cards.back: Major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished on degrees 1 through 7.
cards.example: In C major the chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B diminished.

cards.front: What is Diatonic triad qualities in natural minor?
cards.back: Minor, diminished, major, minor, minor, major, major on degrees 1 through 7.
cards.example: In A natural minor the fifth-degree triad is E minor.

cards.front: What is Dominant triad in harmonic minor?
cards.back: A major triad on the fifth degree, created by raising the scale's seventh degree.
cards.example: A harmonic minor uses E, G-sharp, B as its dominant triad.

cards.back: A phrase-ending progression from dominant harmony to tonic, commonly V to I or V to i.
cards.example: G major moving to C major can make an authentic cadence in C.

cards.back: In common-practice analysis, V to I with both chords in root position and the tonic in the final soprano.
cards.example: A root-position G chord resolves to root-position C with C highest.

cards.back: A phrase ending on dominant harmony.
cards.example: A phrase in C major ends on G major.

cards.back: A cadence moving from subdominant to tonic, conventionally IV to I.
cards.example: F major moves to C major at a phrase ending.

cards.back: A dominant resolves to an unexpected harmony instead of the expected tonic, commonly V to vi in major.
cards.example: G major moves to A minor in C major.

cards.back: A dominant-function chord directed toward a temporary tonic other than the main tonic.
cards.example: D7 acts as V of V when it leads to G in C major.

cards.back: A change from one established key to another.
cards.example: A piece moves from C major into a sustained G major section.

cards.back: A temporary emphasis on a chord as a local tonic without necessarily establishing a lasting new key.
cards.example: A brief D7 to G in C major tonicizes G.

cards.back: The speed of the musical beat.
cards.example: A metronome marking of quarter note = 80 specifies eighty quarter-note beats per minute.

cards.back: A recurring pulse used to organize musical time.
cards.example: A listener taps a steady beat while a melody has varied note lengths.

cards.back: The pattern of durations and timing of notes and rests.
cards.example: Two eighth notes followed by a quarter note form a rhythmic pattern.

cards.back: The organization of beats into recurring groups with patterns of relative emphasis.
cards.example: Triple meter groups beats in threes.

cards.back: A notation indicating the metrical organization, often using two numbers at the beginning of a piece.
cards.example: 4/4 indicates four quarter-note units per full measure.

cards.back: Meter in which each main beat normally divides into two equal parts.
cards.example: In 2/4, each quarter-note beat divides into two eighth notes.

cards.back: Meter in which each main beat normally divides into three equal parts.
cards.example: In 6/8, each dotted-quarter beat divides into three eighth notes.

cards.back: Meter organized around two main beats per measure.
cards.example: 2/4 is simple duple and 6/8 is compound duple.

cards.back: Meter organized around three main beats per measure.
cards.example: 3/4 is simple triple and 9/8 is compound triple.

cards.back: Meter organized around four main beats per measure.
cards.example: 4/4 is simple quadruple and 12/8 is compound quadruple.

cards.back: A duration equal to two half notes or four quarter notes, regardless of which note value receives the beat.
cards.example: A whole note fills a normal 4/4 measure.

cards.back: A duration equal to two quarter notes.
cards.example: Two half notes fill a normal 4/4 measure.

cards.back: A duration equal to two eighth notes or one quarter of a whole note.
cards.example: Four quarter notes fill a normal 4/4 measure.

cards.back: A duration equal to half a quarter note or two sixteenth notes.
cards.example: Two eighth notes equal one quarter note.

cards.back: A duration equal to one quarter of a quarter note.
cards.example: Four sixteenth notes equal one quarter note.

cards.back: A dot after a note or rest that adds half of its original duration.
cards.example: A dotted quarter note equals three eighth notes.

cards.back: A note with added durations of one half and one quarter of its undotted value, totaling seven quarters of that value.
cards.example: A double-dotted half note equals seven eighth notes.

cards.back: Three notes performed in the time ordinarily occupied by two notes of the same written value in a simple-meter subdivision.
cards.example: Three eighth-note triplets take the time of one quarter note.

cards.back: Rhythmic emphasis on normally weak beats or subdivisions, or continuation across an expected strong accent.
cards.example: A note begins on an offbeat and is tied across the next downbeat.

cards.back: One or more pickup notes before the first full measure or principal downbeat.
cards.example: A melody begins with one quarter-note pickup before a 4/4 bar.

cards.back: The first beat of a measure, often the strongest metrical position.
cards.example: Beat one in 3/4 is the downbeat.

cards.back: A weak part of the beat or a normally less-accented metrical position, depending on context.
cards.example: The and between numbered beats is a common offbeat subdivision.

cards.front: What is Piano as a dynamic marking?
cards.back: Soft; commonly abbreviated p.
cards.example: A passage marked p is played softly relative to its context.

cards.front: What is Forte as a dynamic marking?
cards.back: Loud; commonly abbreviated f.
cards.example: A passage marked f is played loudly relative to its context.

cards.back: Moderately soft; abbreviated mp.
cards.example: mp generally calls for more sound than p in the same context.

cards.back: Moderately loud; abbreviated mf.
cards.example: mf generally calls for less sound than f in the same context.

cards.back: Very soft; abbreviated pp.
cards.example: A quiet echo effect may be marked pp.

cards.back: Very loud; abbreviated ff.
cards.example: A powerful climax may be marked ff.

cards.back: A gradual increase in loudness.
cards.example: A phrase grows from p toward f.

cards.back: A gradual decrease in loudness; often used similarly to decrescendo.
cards.example: A phrase fades from f toward p.

cards.back: Smoothly connected articulation.
cards.example: A melody is played without noticeable gaps between adjacent notes.

cards.back: Detached articulation, usually indicated by dots; exact note shortening depends on style.
cards.example: A sequence of staccato notes has clear separation.

cards.back: An emphasis on a note, often through a stronger attack or greater prominence.
cards.example: An accented offbeat stands out from surrounding notes.

cards.back: A gradual slowing of tempo.
cards.example: A closing phrase slows before its final chord.

cards.back: A gradual speeding up of tempo.
cards.example: A repeated pattern becomes progressively faster.

cards.back: Return to the preceding or indicated main tempo after a change.
cards.example: After a ritardando, a tempo restores the earlier speed.

cards.back: Expressive flexibility in timing, with the precise practice depending on style and context.
cards.example: A performer subtly stretches one phrase and relaxes the next.

cards.back: A single melodic line without independent harmonic accompaniment, even if doubled in unison or octaves.
cards.example: A group sings the same melody together without chords.

cards.back: A texture with one main melodic line supported by accompaniment or coordinated chordal parts.
cards.example: A melody over strummed chords is homophonic.

cards.back: Two or more simultaneously sounding, relatively independent melodic lines.
cards.example: A fugue combines independent melodic voices.

cards.back: A form with two principal sections, commonly described as AB.
cards.example: A dance presents an A section followed by a contrasting B section.

cards.back: A form with three main sections in an ABA pattern, including a return of the opening material.
cards.example: A contrasting middle section is followed by the opening theme again.

cards.back: A form in which a recurring main section alternates with contrasting episodes.
cards.example: ABACA is a common rondo plan.
